rendering_architecture: ONE decision governs this whole file and is stated once here. The blanket partition is rendered STRUCTURALLY -- off attested POSITION words and attested STATE words (Sanskrit antar / bahis + avasthā; Latin interior / exterior + status; Hindi āntarik / bāhya + avasthā) -- and NEVER off substance words. The reason: the MIND concept's own note names the danger, which is that a register will render μ with a word for mind (manas, citta, ātman, mens, animus) and thereby assert an experiencer that the mathematics does not contain and the corpus explicitly disclaims. The same logic bans world-words for η (loka, jagat, mundus) and body-words for b (śarīra, kāya, corpus). The resulting renderings are deliberately flat and slightly awkward. FLATNESS IS THE FEATURE: a set of states is what the formalism contains, the formalism admits partitions for a Newton's cradle and a burning fuse, and a rendering elegant enough to sound like a person has falsified the concept in the act of translating it. Every substance-word that a competent translator would reach for is recorded in forbidden_mistranslations with the reason and, where retrieved, the lexicon's own gloss against it.

expected_coinage_note: THE CHARTER'S PREDICTION HELD, and the exact shape of it is worth recording. Sanskrit and Latin technical vocabulary for modern mathematics largely DOES NOT EXIST as attested classical terms, and this file found none: ALL 14 Sanskrit registers are COINED, and across all 56 non-English registers exactly ONE is CITED -- the Latin BODY (superficies), the only headword used as its lexicon carries it. 17 Sanskrit and 11 Latin headwords were retrieved and they were all consumed as COMPONENTS of coinages, not as terms. The clearest case is CONDITIONAL_MUTUAL_INFORMATION: there is NO word for Shannon information in either classical language, because the quantity was defined in 1948. Where a genuine classical term DID fit -- avasthā (state), antar (within), bahis (outside), status, interior, exterior, superficies, lapsus, skhalana, paraspara, mutuus -- it was used and cited. Where none fitted, a coinage was made and labelled a coinage. No attested word was pretended to mean a modern technical term.
doctrinal_freight_note: Sanskrit philosophical vocabulary carries DOCTRINAL FREIGHT: a Sāṃkhya or Vedānta term imports a whole metaphysics. This file's ambiguity_notes are where that is recorded, per CONCEPTS.json's own instruction. The four sharpest instances found, each grounded in retrieved lexicon text: (1) āvaraṇa for the blanket -- Monier-Williams gives 'covering, hiding, concealing' and the Jain 'mental blindness'; in Advaita it names māyā's veiling power, so it would assert a real hidden world, i.e. make the FRISTON_BLANKET claim true by vocabulary. (2) manas for μ -- Monier-Williams itself glosses it 'the internal organ or antaḥkaraṇa of perception and cognition ... by which objects of sense affect the soul', which installs a soul. (3) saṃyoga for mind.body -- correct as a RELATION (a Nyāya guṇa, not a dravya), but the same entry glosses it 'direct material contact' and it presupposes substances to inhere in. (4) indriya for sensory states -- an ORGAN, and in Vedānta one of fourteen including manas, buddhi, ahaṃkāra and citta, each with a presiding deity. In no case has this file let a translation choice quietly assert a metaphysics; in every case the freight is named and left unresolved for an expert.

ambiguity_notes: vyavadhāna carries 'obstruction, hiding from view' alongside 'intervening'. The blanket does NOT hide the world from the mind and does not obstruct anything; it MEDIATES. A reader taking the concealment sense has been handed the Friston reading (a real thing being hidden behind a real surface) at no evidential cost. This is the reason the term is admitted with its definition attached and never alone.
vyavadhāna also carries 'cessation, termination' and, in grammar, the very narrow 'intervention of a syllable or letter'. Neither is meant.

velamen is a CLOTH word - a veil or garment. It therefore renders the English metaphor faithfully, which is precisely the risk: it reproduces 'blanket' rather than repairing it. Per the source concept's own note, this register is rendering a METAPHOR, not a mechanism, and that fact is recorded here rather than smoothed over.

'Blanket' in English is already a bad metaphor for b: a blanket on a bed covers by lying on top and does its work by hiding. b does its work by conditioning. Every register inherits this defect from the English and none of them repairs it. The definition, not the word, is the object.
The name 'Markov' attaches to a construct Markov did not define in this form; the term is eponymous convention, and no register should be read as a claim about Markov's own work.

forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: Monier-Williams gives āvaraṇa as 'covering, hiding, concealing'; 'the act of covering, concealing, hiding'; 'an obstruction'; and, in the Jain sense, 'mental blindness'. Rendering the blanket āvaraṇa asserts that b CONCEALS η from μ. It does not. Worse: in Advaita Vedānta āvaraṇa names māyā's veiling power, which hides a reality that IS there. That single word therefore smuggles in (a) a real external world, (b) the claim that it is hidden, and (c) a Vedānta metaphysics - i.e. it asserts the FRISTON_BLANKET reading by vocabulary alone, in a corpus that explicitly declines it. This is the worst available rendering and it is also the most natural one.

Tempting, because Vedānta uses upādhi for a limiting adjunct and b does limit. But Monier-Williams gives its primary sense as 'that which is put in the place of another thing, a substitute, substitution', and it also carries 'appearance, phantom' and 'deception'. b is not a substitute for anything and is not an illusion; in the Advaita usage the adjunct is precisely what is to be SEEN THROUGH, which inverts the concept - b is the only thing there is to see.

McGregor gives कंबल kambal, m., as 'a blanket' - the textile, the thing on a bed. This is the literal calque a translator or a machine reaches for first, and it renders a conditional-independence structure as bedding. It is the single most plausible failure in this register.

Both are 'covering' words reached for by the same cloth instinct as velamen but WITHOUT even velamen's advantage of being the conventional calque. back_translation_test.test: Present the target-register term TOGETHER WITH its literal gloss, but WITHOUT the English term and WITHOUT the formal definition, to 3 independent readers competent in that register and naive to this corpus. Ask: (1) render this into English; (2) state what relation, if any, it asserts between the thing inside and the thing outside.
back_translation_test.pass_criterion: PASS iff 3/3 return an English rendering naming a covering/screen associated with Markov, AND 0/3 answer question (2) with a concealment relation ('it hides the outside from the inside', 'the outside is really there but veiled'). ANY concealment answer is a FAIL for that register and forces the term back to the coinage bench, because concealment is the FRISTON_BLANKET claim and this corpus does not make it.

ambiguity_notes: This is the operator's fourth term and the load-bearing one, and the whole difficulty is grammatical rather than lexical: mind.body is a RELATION, not a thing. M12 leaves it implicit. Every register in this entry is therefore built as a PHRASE (genitive/postposition), never as a compound noun, because a compound noun in any of these languages would name a third substance - and naming a third substance is how you reopen dualism, which the partition does not contain.

That is why the Latin is a five-word phrase rather than an elegant single word. The elegance would be the defect. Any reviewer tempted to compress 'coniunctio statuum interiorum cum superficie' into something like 'menticorpus' or 'animocorporeum' has, in the act of compressing, asserted the thing this entry exists to deny.

saṃyoga was chosen because Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika treats it as a RELATION (a guṇa inhering in substances), not as a substance - which is precisely right. But the freight is heavy and cuts both ways: to treat saṃyoga as a guṇa is to accept an ontology in which qualities inhere in SUBSTANCES, i.e. it presupposes that μ and b are substances that can bear qualities. They are sets of states. The register buys the correct relation-type at the price of an incorrect substance-metaphysics. This is exactly the doctrinal-freight problem the charter names and it is NOT resolved here.

Monier-Williams gives indriya as 'faculty of sense, sense, organ of sense' - an ORGAN or POWER belonging to a cognizer, not a state. Its Vedāntic sense is worse: the entry records fourteen indriya-s comprising five sense organs, five motor organs, PLUS manas, buddhi, ahaṃkāra and citta, each governed by a presiding deity. Rendering s as indriya therefore (a) makes s an organ rather than a state, (b) installs the very cognizer that MIND forbids, and (c) imports a fourteen-fold psychology with deities attached. It also collapses SENSORY_STATES and ACTIVE_STATES into one category, since the indriya-s comprise both jn̄ānendriya (sense) and karmendriya (action) - destroying the exact distinction μ/η sparsity depends on.

Independently of the philosophy: Monier-Williams's PRIMARY senses for indriya are 'power, force, the quality which belongs especially to the mighty Indra', 'exhibition of power, powerful act', 'bodily power', 'virile power', and 'semen virile'. The word is built on the god Indra. A translator using it for 's' is not reaching for a neutral technical term; they are reaching for a word whose core sense is divine potency.

Lewis & Short gives sensus, us, m. as 'the faculty or power of perceiving; perception, feeling, sensation, sense', and its whole section II is mental - 'feeling, sentiment, emotion, affection; sense, understanding, capacity; humor, inclination, disposition, frame of mind', plus 'opinion, thought, view' and sensus communis. 'Perception' and 'observation' both name an ACT performed by a subject; s is a set of states, and the act-reading reinstalls the subject. 'Input' is the mirror error: it is engineering-neutral but implies an intended recipient and a designed channel, and it invites the reading that s is data delivered to μ. Nothing delivers anything. s is simply the part of b that η influences and μ does not.

ambiguity_notes: The source concept is emphatic and the emphasis is the content: NOT 'mostly' and NOT 'usually' - by definition, or the partition is not a blanket. Every register must carry an exact factorization claim, not a tendency. No natural-language word for 'independent' in any of these registers carries exactness; they all admit degrees. This is a defect of all five registers equally and the math is the only fence.

The deep trap, and the reason this entry is hard: 'independence' in ordinary language is a property of ONE thing (a person is independent). Here it is a three-place relation - μ is independent of η GIVEN b - and it is FALSE without the third place. Drop 'given b' and the claim becomes not merely weaker but wrong: μ and η are emphatically NOT independent unconditionally; that is exactly why there is a blanket. A register that renders this with a one-place word for independence has stated the opposite of the concept.

The Sanskrit coinage is designed against exactly that failure: by yoking sāpekṣa ('dependent, having regard to') to nirapekṣa ('independent, without regard to') - the two morphological opposites of a single root - it makes the conditionality structurally inseparable from the independence. You cannot drop the third place without dropping half the word. This is the one place in the file where a coinage does something no attested term does.

nirapekṣa's freight is severe and pulls the wrong way: Monier-Williams's other senses are 'desireless, careless, indifferent, disinterested', and the adverb nirapekṣam is 'regardlessly, ACCIDENTALLY'. That makes independence an ATTITUDE (not caring about something) rather than a probabilistic factorization, and the 'accidentally' sense is close to a direct contradiction: conditional independence is not an accident but a structural fact. A reader with the Mānava-dharmaśāstra or Kāvya usage in mind will hear an ascetic's detachment where a factorization is meant.
sāpekṣa's attested sense 'having regard or respect to' is also personal - it is about someone showing consideration. Neither component is a mathematical term and neither pretends to be.

forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: The cardinal error of this entry and the most likely one. μ and η are NOT independent; they are independent GIVEN b. A bare independence word asserts unconditional independence, which is false and which, if true, would mean there was nothing to infer and no reason for a blanket to exist. This is not a shade of meaning - it is the negation of the concept.

'Self-dependence, autonomy, freedom' - a one-place property of an agent, and in Śaiva and grammatical usage a term of art for AGENCY (the kāraka svatantraḥ kartā, 'the agent is the independent one'). It therefore commits both available errors at once: it drops the conditioning term, and it installs an agent. Both are the classical idiom for independence and both are POLITICAL or LEGAL - freedom from another's power, being one's own master. Statistical factorization has nothing to do with either. Listed as traps; NOT retrieved from Lewis & Short.

'Uncorrelated' is a strictly weaker condition than independence (zero correlation does not imply independence except in special cases) and substituting it silently weakens the claim to something the blanket does not require and which would not suffice. ambiguity_notes: THE HONEST OUTCOME THE CHARTER PREDICTS, arriving exactly where it was predicted: there is NO attested Sanskrit term and NO attested Latin term for information in Shannon's sense. None. The quantity was defined in 1948 and neither language has a word for it. Every register in this entry is therefore a coinage or a calque, and the ONLY thing in this entry with any warrant is the mathematics: I(μ;η|b), measured in NATS. The unit is the fence. No register may be read as supplying a meaning the math does not already carry.

Latin informatio is the trap of this entry, and it is a beautiful one because the word is CITED, classical, and Ciceronian - and means something else entirely. Lewis & Short: 'an outline, sketch, first draft' and, tropologically, 'an idea, conception'. Cicero uses it at N.D. 1.36.100 for a PRECONCEIVED NOTION in someone's mind. Cicero's informatio is a mental conception in a person; Shannon's information is a measure over a joint distribution and requires no mind at all. Using informatio therefore imports a cognizer into the one entry whose whole job is to be a mind-free measurement. The word looks like the right answer and is an anachronism of two thousand years.

mutuus's primary attested sense is 'borrowed, lent', with the substantive mutuum meaning 'a loan'; the 'reciprocal, mutual' sense is marked Transf. (transferred) by Lewis & Short, and its gloss there opens 'in return, in exchange'. informatio mutua could therefore be construed as 'a borrowed conception' - a loan of an idea. This is not a serious reading risk in context but it is what the lexicon actually says, and it is recorded rather than quietly dropped. ADVERSARY CORRECTION 2026-07-15: this note previously said the sense is 'marked Trop. by Lewis & Short'. It is marked Transf. The note's SUBSTANCE survives the correction unchanged - 'borrowed, lent' is still the literal sense and 'mutual' is still the transferred one - but the label was wrong and a note that names what a lexicon marks must name it correctly.

Hindi sūcanā is the everyday modern word for 'information' as in a notice, an announcement, something someone tells you. That is the folk sense, not the measure-theoretic one, and it is arguably the worst kind of false friend: it will feel entirely natural to a Hindi reader and will convey nothing of I(μ;η|b). Because sūcanā's Hindi sense is a communication BETWEEN PERSONS, it also reinstalls the cognizer.

THE SCOPE FACT THAT MATTERS MOST, carried from the source concept and softened by nobody: this criterion exists, is clean, and is overwhelmingly UNEXERCISED. I(μ;η|b) is NOT-MEASURED for essentially all real biological systems and for every UNI boundary. When any text says 'system X has a Markov blanket', the default assumption should be that I was never estimated. Naming this quantity elegantly in five registers does not measure it in one.

The nats are load-bearing and no register carries them. I > 0 beyond ESTIMATOR NOISE is the operable test; the noise floor is part of the claim; a term without a unit and an error bar is not a measurement.

Rendering information as jn̄āna installs a knower in the one place a knower is most damaging, and vijn̄āna additionally imports the whole Yogācāra apparatus. ambiguity_notes: ATTESTATION HONESTY, carried from the source concept and applying to this file's own English: the corpus writes this as 'blankets of blankets' / 'Nesting'. The hyphenated term 'blanket-nesting' appears in 0 FILES of the corpus. The English headword being translated here is therefore itself a lexicon-internal coinage, and the four other registers are translations of a term the corpus does not actually use. Recorded because it would be easy to present this entry as though the English were settled.

THE DISTINCTION THIS ENTRY EXISTS TO PROTECT: that blankets CAN compose this way is a MATHEMATICAL FACT. That any particular biological hierarchy IS so composed is a SEPARATE EMPIRICAL CLAIM. And the number of nested levels in any named organism is NOT-MEASURED. The concept is a CONSTRUCTION, not an observation. The organelle-cell-tissue-organ-organism-colony-ecosystem ladder is an illustration of a possibility, not a report of a finding - and it reads exactly like a report of a finding, in all five registers.

garbha is the contested choice in this file and the argument runs both ways. FOR: Monier-Williams attests 'the inside, middle, interior of anything' and 'any interior chamber, adytum or sanctuary of a temple' - the garbhagṛha of a temple is literally a chamber nested inside a larger structure, which is the right image. AGAINST: the entry's FIRST sense is 'the womb', and it also carries 'a foetus or embryo, child, brood or offspring (of birds)' and 'a woman's courses'. The reproductive senses dominate the entry. A reader will hear gestation, and nesting is composition, not reproduction: the inner blanket is not the outer blanket's offspring and is not developing into anything.

The bird sense of garbha ('brood or offspring OF BIRDS') collides with the English metaphor in a way that looks helpful and is not: English 'nesting' is already a bird metaphor, and a reader may take the convergence as confirmation. It is a coincidence of two unrelated metaphors, and taking it as confirmation would be exactly the kind of false comfort this file is built to refuse.

The Latin refuses a nesting-noun entirely and uses recursive syntax instead. This is the file's only register that carries recursion by GRAMMAR rather than by LEXICON, and it is the more honest solution for a concept whose content is a structural relation.

What no register carries: the DIRECTION of the recursion (one level's BLANKET becomes the next level's INTERNAL STATES - a b becomes a μ, which is a type change, not merely a containment). 'Screens within screens' says containment and says nothing about the type change. The definition does.

forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: The direct calque of English 'nesting' and firmly refused. Lewis & Short gives nidus as 'a nest' (Cic. de Or. 2.6.23; Verg. G. 4.307), with transferred senses 'young birds in a nest', 'a litter of pigs', 'a receptacle or case for books', 'a dwelling, residence, home'. Every one is a CONTAINER OR A HOME - a physical thing that holds another physical thing, with a bird in it. Blanket nesting is a recursive type relation in which one level's blanket becomes the next level's internal states. nidus imports birds, dwellings and litters and conveys no recursion at all. That the English word 'nesting' is itself this metaphor is the defect being repaired here, not a licence to reproduce it in Latin.
The Sanskrit bird's-nest word - same defect as nidus. NOT retrieved from Monier-Williams by this file; the gloss is the author's and is NOT cited.

forbidden_mistranslations.wrong: any rendering implying the inner level is the outer level's offspring, or is developing/gestating
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: The garbha risk made explicit, and the reason this entry's Sanskrit is only provisionally admitted. Nesting is COMPOSITION. The inner blanket is not born from the outer one, is not growing, and is not becoming anything.

forbidden_mistranslations.wrong: any rendering implying the biological ladder is an observed hierarchy
forbidden_mistranslations.why_wrong: Not lexical but evidential, and the most consequential error available here. That blankets CAN nest is mathematics; that a given organism's levels DO is an unmade measurement. The number of nested levels in any named organism is NOT-MEASURED.

All three are theory-laden imports. 'Hierarchy' adds control and rank, which the relation does not contain; 'levels of organisation' imports a whole biological research programme; 'emergence' asserts a contested thesis the concept does not make. The relation is composition, full stop.

back_translation_test.test: Present the target-register expression and its literal gloss, with NO English term and NO definition, to 3 independent readers competent in that register and naive to this corpus. Ask: (1) render into English; (2) does this describe something being contained in something of the same kind, or something being born from / growing inside something else? (3) does this expression assert that any real organism is built this way?
back_translation_test.pass_criterion: PASS iff 3/3 answer (2) 'contained in something of the same kind'; AND 3/3 answer (3) 'no'. A gestation/birth answer to (2) is a FAIL and is the PREDICTED failure for the SANSKRIT specifically, since garbha's dominant attested senses are womb, foetus and offspring - if it fails, garbha must be struck and replaced, and this file records in advance that it expects to lose that argument. A 'yes' to (3) is a FAIL in every register: the construction has been read as an observation, which is the evidential error this entry exists to prevent.
